case_info.scenario: A 69-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of progressive skin discoloration. His medical history included chronic kidney disease, chronic hepatitis C infection, cirrhosis, ischemic cardiomyopathy with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), and atrial fibrillation with prophylactic apixaban. He had recurrent staphylococcus bacteremia due to infection of an ICD lead and had been treated for the past 6 months with minocycline, 100 mg twice daily. His arms had been purple and bruise-like for several years but turned a near black color 1 month ago. He reported no discoloration of his sweat or urine. He had no history of malnutrition and reported infrequent alcohol use. Physical examination showed dense blue-black skin pigmentation of his forearms, dorsal hands, legs, and dorsal feet, as well as blue discoloration of his sclerae and teeth (Figure 1). He had normal-colored nails and oral mucosa. Laboratory studies showed white blood cell count of 15 800/μL (reference range, 4000-11 000/μL), hemoglobin of 10.7 g/dL (reference, 13.5-17.5 g/dL), platelet count of 58 000/μL (reference, 150 000-400 000/μL), and INR of 1.8 (reference, 0.8-1.1). Complete metabolic panel showed increased creatinine (1.51 mg/dL; reference, 0.64-1.27 mg/dL) and elevated total bilirubin (1.7 mg/dL; reference range, 0.3-1.2 mg/dL). His estimated glomerular filtration rate was 40 mL/min/1.73 m2.
case_info.explanation: The keys to the correct diagnosis are the blue-black color of the pigmentation, the location on the distal extremities, and the involvement of sclerae and teeth. Potential etiologies for blue skin discoloration include drug-induced (eg, amiodarone, minocycline, hydroxychloroquine, and fluoroquinolones1), exposure to silver (argyria) or gold salts (chrysiasis), and deposition of pigmented fibers due to an inherited enzyme deficiency (endogenous ochronosis or alkaptonuria) or hydroquinone use (exogenous ochronosis).2Given this patient’s ongoing minocycline use, discontinuing minocycline is the best answer. This patient’s ecchymoses, most prominent at his proximal forearms, represent a distinct process from the blue-black pigmentation caused by minocycline. The ecchymoses were due to his use of apixaban, thrombocytopenia, bleeding diathesis, and skin fragility from age and sun exposure and would not necessitate stopping apixaban (choice A). Hemochromatosis (choice C) causes skin dyspigmentation that is typically diffuse and brown or slate-gray.3Pellagra, caused by deficiency in niacin (vitamin B3) (choice D), presents with a photodistributed rash; however, the rash is red or brown and does not discolor sclerae or teeth.2 Minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation presents as blue-hued pigmentation of the skin that may also involve the sclerae, nails, teeth, and oral mucosa. The reported incidence varies from 2% to 15% in patients treated for acne to 41% to 54% in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and orthopedic infections, respectively.4-6 Although minocycline-induced cutaneous hyperpigmentation is a clinical diagnosis, skin biopsy can confirm the diagnosis and reveals subepidermal deposition of granular black pigment both interstitially and intracellularly (Figure 2). The pigment reacts positively with staining techniques used to detect iron and/or melanin (Perl’s Prussian blue and Fontana-Masson, respectively). In contrast, ecchymoses stain positive for iron only. While the mechanism of hyperpigmentation remains unclear, histopathologic studies indicate that minocycline and/or its metabolites likely form insoluble complexes with iron that deposit in tissue.7 Minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation is classified into 3 types based on clinical findings and histologic staining, though these categories may overlap. In type I, blue pigmentation is found in scars, commonly facial acne scars, and stains positive for iron only. In type II, blue pigmentation affects normal skin, typically on the extremities, and stains positive for both iron and melanin. Type III presents with muddy brown discoloration most prominent in sun-exposed skin and stains positive for melanin.8 This patient’s presentation was consistent with type II hyperpigmentation and notable for both the striking degree of pigmentation and for its rapid development after only 6 months of treatment. Most minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation occurs after a year, though small case series have reported pigmentation after only a few weeks.5,6,9Several characteristics of this patient may have contributed to the more rapid onset, including the longstanding purpura on his arms, which increases dermal iron available for chelation, as well as hepatic and kidney disease, which impair drug metabolism and excretion. Minocycline-induced cutaneous hyperpigmentation persists after drug cessation and is challenging to treat. Given the small size of the pigment particle, treatment is best approached with picosecond or Q-switched lasers.10In addition to its effects on skin pigmentation, minocycline use in children can result in permanent teeth discoloration and bone hypoplasia and should be avoided during pregnancy and in children younger than 8 years old.2 Minocycline was discontinued and daptomycin was started in its place. The patient declined treatment for the pigmentation changes because they were not bothersome to him.
